card.hook: From the street, St John's looks like a fortress that forgot to dress for the party. Don't be fooled, because the inside is gold, carved and wildly over the top.
card.stand_here: The phone icon on the map sits right at the building. For the front, walk out into the street or square outside and step back until both bell towers fit, facing the façade.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x for the façade, which keeps the stone looking calm and not stretched. Inside, switch to zoom 0.5x for the nave and the painted ceiling. If your phone has 2x or 5x, use it for carved details and the ceiling figures.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the two bell towers up with them so the façade doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Early or late in the day is often quieter, so you can shoot the inside without a crowd in the frame. It's dim in there, so your phone may switch to night mode. Hold it steady with your elbows tucked in.
card.selfie_here: Stand in St John's Square, where the main entrance is, and face back toward the limestone front. Use the front camera (try 0.5x if your phone has it) and let the façade sit behind your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: No flash inside, and personal photos are generally allowed in the nave and chapels. The Oratory (the Caravaggio room) may be restricted, so check the policy at the entrance and on the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find a painted figure beside a column that fools you into thinking it's a real statue, then get a photo where you can't tell either.
card.good_to_know: The Order of St John built the cathedral between 1573 and 1578, designed by Maltese architect Girolamo Cassar. In the 1660s Mattia Preti redecorated the inside in rich Baroque style, with a painted ceiling showing scenes from the life of John the Baptist. The marble floor is a patchwork of tombs, said to hold about 400 knights and officers of the Order.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: The phone icon on the map sits right at the building. For the front, walk out into the street or square outside and step back until both bell towers fit, facing the façade.

card.hook: Everyone at Upper Barrakka Gardens heads straight for the big open terrace, and then they all take the same photo. Walk to the far end of the garden instead, where the stone arches turn the Grand Harbour into a row of tiny framed pictures.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, in the colonnaded arcades at the end of the garden. Step into the line of arches and face along them, so they lead your eye towards the harbour.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole run of arches in. Then try 1x for a calmer, less stretched look, and 2x to pick out the harbour through a single arch.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines and keep your phone level, so the columns stand up nice and straight.
card.best_time: After sunset is the best time, when the arcades are lit and the stone has a warm glow. If you'd rather shoot the terrace, go early to beat the crowd.
card.selfie_here: Sit under the stone arches of the arcade inside the gardens, with the harbour framed through the openings behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x so the arches fit over your shoulder. It's far less photographed than the standard terrace shot, so you should get a less crowded backdrop.
card.rules_and_safety: The cannon firing at the Saluting Battery is loud and can startle you, so hold your phone tightly if you film it.
card.challenge: Find an arch where the harbour fills the opening like a tiny postcard, and get the whole frame straight with no tilted columns.
card.good_to_know: The gardens sit on top of Saints Peter and Paul Bastion, built in the 1560s, at the highest point of Valletta's city walls. The Italian knight Fra Flaminio Balbiani built the arches in 1661. They were roofed at first, and the ceiling came off after the Rising of the Priests in 1775, which is why they're open to the sky today.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, in the colonnaded arcades at the end of the garden. Step into the line of arches and face along them, so they lead your eye towards the harbour.

card.hook: From the top terrace at Upper Barrakka Gardens, Fort St Elmo looks like a pale, pointy arrowhead stuck into the very end of Valletta. It's a small shape at first, but once you spot it you can't unsee it.
card.stand_here: Stand on the upper terrace of Upper Barrakka Gardens, a free public garden, and face across the harbour to the fort at the tip of the land. Lower Barrakka Gardens is a quieter spot with a similar angle if the terrace is busy.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to see how the fort sits in the harbour. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to bring the walls and bastions closer. Skip 0.5x here, because the fort will look tiny.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the fort on a lower third and let the water fill the rest, then tap the fort and slide a little darker so the sky and water keep their colour.
card.best_time: Try the afternoon, when the sun is likely behind you and lights up the fort's walls. Early in the day the garden is likely to be quieter, but the low sun in front of you can make the fort look dark.
card.selfie_here: Try the sea-side path outside the fort. Walk the sea-facing edge, then turn back toward the walls so they sit behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more wall in, and hold the phone a little above eye level. One guide suggests this view, but it isn't a marked selfie spot, so just have a play.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the harbour viewpoint in Upper Barrakka Gardens, where they can frame the whole fort across the water, while you stand between them and the view.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography for personal use is generally permitted in most public areas of the fort and the National War Museum, but flash may be restricted near delicate exhibits. Parts of the fort may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site first. Expect wind on the outer edge.
card.challenge: Get the whole fort in the frame with a strip of harbour and waterfront, so it looks like it's really at the end of the land.
card.good_to_know: Fort St Elmo's defenders held out for 28 days in the Great Siege of 1565 before it fell on 23 June. That delay gave the Knights time to prepare other defences and wait for reinforcements. The first air raid on Malta, on 11 June 1940, struck here, and restoration work finished in 2015.

card.hook: Here's the twist: Fort St Angelo isn't in Valletta at all. It sits on the tip of Birgu in the middle of the Grand Harbour, so the best photo of it is from across the water.
card.stand_here: Stand on the upper terrace at Upper Barrakka Gardens, on the Valletta side above the Grand Harbour, and face south-east. The fort is across the water, with Birgu and Senglea around it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the whole harbour scene. The fort looks fairly small from here, so then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for a closer shot. Skip 0.5x unless you want lots of terrace and sky, because it shrinks the fort to a dot.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the fort, then slide the brightness down a little if the sky is bright, so the pale stone keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the stonework. Check the light on the day, as it changes with the season.
card.selfie_here: Inside the fort, head for the corner of the harbour-side bastion beside the small stone Vedette, the first proper viewpoint after the entry tunnel and lower courtyards. Use the front camera at 0.5x and fit the Vedette and the harbour mouth over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: On Vittoriosa marina, right below the fort walls, ask someone to shoot up at the walls so the whole fort fills the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The fort itself may be ticketed or have restricted areas, so check the official site before you go. Wear comfortable shoes, as the route has uneven surfaces throughout.
card.challenge: Put the fort a little off-centre, let the harbour water fill the bottom of the frame, and use the gridlines to get the horizon dead level.
card.good_to_know: The fort began as a medieval castle called Castrum Maris, the 'Castle by the Sea'. The Order of Saint John rebuilt it between the 1530s and 1560s, and it was their headquarters in the Great Siege of 1565. The British garrisoned it from 1800 to 1979, and it has been on Malta's tentative UNESCO World Heritage list since 1998.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the upper terrace at Upper Barrakka Gardens, on the Valletta side above the Grand Harbour, and face south-east. The fort is across the water, with Birgu and Senglea around it.

card.hook: The Grandmaster's Palace fills a whole city block, yet its front is plain and a bit stern, and it isn't even perfectly symmetrical. All those changes over the centuries left you strong lines and lots of texture to photograph.
card.stand_here: Stand in Misraħ San Ġorġ (St George's Square), right in front of the palace, and face the long façade. The clock tower and fountains should be in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole frontage in. Then switch to 1x for a more natural, less stretched look. For the balconies, doorways and carved stonework, try 2x to 5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the roofline up with a horizontal line so the long wall doesn't tilt, and keep the phone upright.
card.best_time: Go early in the day if you want fewer people in the square. If you're passing more than once, take a few shots at different times and pick your favourite.
card.selfie_here: Try the street corner on Republic Street, across from the red phone box, so the wooden balconies hang overhead. Use the front camera at 0.5x, hold it a little high, and check the screen to see how much palace made it in behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in St George's Square facing the palace front, roughly 90 m from the phone icon on the map. You stand near the palace so the whole frontage fits behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally allowed in the public areas, but check signs for restrictions, and flash may be limited. The State Rooms and Armoury inside are a Heritage Malta museum, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the red phone box and the wooden balconies in one frame, with the balconies sitting nice and straight.
card.good_to_know: The palace was built between the 16th and 18th centuries for the Grand Master of the Knights Hospitaller, who ruled Malta from 1530 to 1798. Later it was the British governor's residence, then the seat of Parliament. Today it houses the Office of the President of Malta.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Misraħ San Ġorġ (St George's Square), right in front of the palace, and face the long façade. The clock tower and fountains should be in front of you.

card.hook: Three bronze sea gods are holding up a giant basin while buses rumble past, and somehow it all works. Tritons' Fountain is the first big hello you get at Valletta's City Gate.
card.stand_here: Stand on City Gate bridge and face the fountain, with the gate behind you. From this side you can see the faces of the Tritons.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to show the fountain in its square. Go to 0.5x if you want the whole basin and the bastions in one frame. Zoom 2x or more (depending on your phone) to pick out the bronze Tritons.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the bronze figures, then drag the slider a little darker so the pale stone doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Early evening, once the fountain lights come on. Switch on night mode if the light fades, and tuck your elbows in to keep the shot steady.
card.selfie_here: Try the City Gate bridge, from the gate end, with the fountain in view. Use the front camera and hold your phone out so the whole fountain fills the frame behind you. Try 0.5x if it won't all fit.
card.ask_someone: Ask a friendly passer-by to stand across the roundabout from the fountain, on the bus-terminus side, so all three Tritons fit in one frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Please don't climb the bronze sculptures or step into the water, for safety and to protect them. Take care around the buses and traffic.
card.challenge: Spot the spiral: two Tritons sit and one kneels. Can you frame them so the whole round basin sits near the centre of your gridlines, with no tilt?
card.good_to_know: The fountain was designed and built between 1952 and 1959 by sculptor Vincent Apap and draughtsman Victor Anastasi. It's counted among Malta's most important Modernist landmarks. It reopened after restoration on 12 January 2018, and it sits technically in Floriana, just outside the gate.

card.hook: Picture a pale, four-cornered star fort sitting low in the middle of the harbour, with Valletta stacked up behind it. You get that view for free, just by strolling along a promenade.
card.stand_here: Head for the Gżira seafront, roughly 750 m in a straight line (an estimated 10-15 minute walk), and stand on Triq ix-Xatt, the Gżira waterfront promenade (The Strand). Face across the water towards the bridge to Manoel Island, and the fort's limestone bastions will be right in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole line of bastions with the water in front. Then try zoom 2x or more (depending on your phone) to pick out the walls and the Valletta skyline behind. Zoom 0.5x makes the fort look small and far away, so save it for close shots along the shore.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, tap the pale stonework, then nudge it a little darker so the sky keeps its colour and the walls don't wash out.
card.best_time: Golden hour is the one. The low light warms the limestone walls and the Valletta skyline behind them.
card.selfie_here: Walk over to the outer walls of Fort Manoel on Manoel Island and take your selfie with the stone walls filling the frame behind you. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x if your phone has it so you both fit in. Photo guides mention these walls as a backdrop but don't name an exact spot, so wander along them until the frame looks good.
card.rules_and_safety: The fort's interior is usually closed apart from occasional open days, so plan on exterior photos only. Cars aren't allowed past the island entrance, so you'll walk over the bridge. One guide warns that the island's park closes in the evening, so don't get stuck there.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot and one zoomed shot of the walls, with the waterline on the lower third and the horizon dead level. Then pick your favourite.
card.good_to_know: The Knights Hospitaller built Fort Manoel in the 18th century. It's named after Grand Master António Manoel de Vilhena, who laid the first stone on 14 September 1723. It was meant to protect Valletta's flank from across the water. Later it served the British military until 1964, was badly damaged in the Second World War, and was restored in the early 21st century.

Face across the water towards the bridge to Manoel Island, and the fort's limestone bastions will be right in front of you.

card.hook: Here's a twist: the Barrakka Lift is a bit of a show-off, but it takes better photos as a sidekick than as the star. Let the old stone arcades and the open harbour do the talking, and give the lift a supporting role.
card.stand_here: Stand in Upper Barrakka Gardens, near the entrance and the upper area by the lift's top station. The lift lies to the south from here, so face that way and you'll see its upper end with the garden arcades around it and the harbour opening up behind.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the arcades and the harbour in together. Switch to 1x for a cleaner shot of the top of the lift, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for details like the mesh cladding, as long as the frame doesn't get too tight.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the lift up with a vertical grid line so the shaft stands straight instead of leaning.
card.best_time: Late afternoon or golden hour is the pick, as photo guides suggest for the gardens. The light is kinder on the stone, and the harbour behind looks lovely.
card.selfie_here: Step out onto the Upper Barrakka Gardens harbour terrace, which is overlooking the Grand Harbour and reached by leaving the lift at the top. Use the front camera at 0.5x with the harbour behind you. It's a harbour-view selfie, not a lift-backdrop one, so don't expect the tower in the shot.
card.rules_and_safety: The gardens and the lift are public places, but access to the lift, including hours and fares, can change, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take two or three steps along the terrace between shots and see how the arcades line up differently, then pick your favourite arch to frame the lift.
card.good_to_know: The Barrakka Lift opened in 2012 and stands about 58 metres tall, with a concrete shaft wrapped in aluminium mesh. The ride takes roughly 23 seconds between Lascaris Wharf and the top of the bastion. It replaced an earlier steel lift that ran from 1905 until 1973 and was pulled down in 1983.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Upper Barrakka Gardens, near the entrance and the upper area by the lift's top station. The lift lies to the south from here, so face that way and you'll see its upper end with the garden arcades around it and the harbour opening up behind.

card.hook: Most people walk straight into Lower Barrakka Gardens and miss the best opening shot, which is waiting just outside the gate. It's a big bell, and it makes a surprisingly good foreground.
card.stand_here: Stand at the Siege Bell War Memorial, just outside the garden's southern edge, and turn to look back toward the gardens. Put the bell in front and let the garden and harbour edge sit behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the bell with the gardens behind it. Go to 0.5x for the whole garden and harbour edge (keep important bits away from the edges), or 2x or higher, depending on your phone, to pick out the temple.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the horizon level, then tap the monument and drag it a little darker if the sky is bright so the pale stone keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people. You can shoot here any time of day, though.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera at the stone parapet at the edge of the bastion wall, below the formal garden level. The gardens stay behind you and the harbour view stays open. For a shadier option, try under the arched loggia facing the harbour, with the gardens' architecture over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the garden path facing the Monument to Sir Alexander Ball, with the harbour behind them, while you stand in front of the monument with the arches framing you both.
card.rules_and_safety: Stay on the paths rather than stepping onto planted areas. Parts of the garden can be fenced off during works, so check the official site before you go and be ready to change your view.
card.challenge: Get the bell, the garden and the harbour edge in one level shot with nobody walking through it. Patience is the whole game.
card.good_to_know: The Lower Barrakka Gardens are twinned with the Upper Barrakka Gardens and look out over the Grand Harbour. The Monument to Sir Alexander Ball is a neoclassical temple built in 1810 to honour Malta's first British Civil Commissioner. The gardens were rebuilt in the 1980s and reopened in 2003, and the terrace has plaques for the 1956 Hungarian revolution, the Prague Spring and Giuseppe Garibaldi.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the Siege Bell War Memorial, just outside the garden's southern edge, and turn to look back toward the gardens. Put the bell in front and let the garden and harbour edge sit behind it.

card.hook: Picture a dead-straight street, tall buildings on both sides, and a karozzin rolling right through the middle of your shot. That's Republic Street, and Valletta lined it up for you.
card.stand_here: Keep to the side of the street so you're not in the way of people walking or a passing karozzin.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a natural view down the street, then try 0.5x to fit in the buildings on both sides and lots of sky. For balconies, doorways and shop signs, zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone).
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the street in the centre of the frame and keep your phone level so the tall buildings don't lean.
card.best_time: The street gets busy at Christmas, so allow a little patience if you want a clear view. Whenever you go, wait for a karozzin or electric cab to reach a clear spot in the frame.
card.selfie_here: Climb the stone stairs of Parliament House, where Republic Street begins near City Gate. Use the front camera (try 0.5x if your phone has it) so the modern Renzo Piano-designed stairs are behind you and the street opens up over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Stay to the side of the street so you don't block people walking or the karozzini and electric cabs.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot down the street, then go small: find one balcony or doorway you love and zoom in on it.
card.good_to_know: Republic Street runs about 1 kilometre from City Gate towards Fort St. Elmo. The Order of St. John laid Valletta out on a grid after the Great Siege, and this street sits in the middle of that plan. It has also been called Strada San Giorgio, Strada Reale and Kingsway, and it was heavily bombed in World War II. Today it's mostly pedestrianised, with only karozzini and electric cabs allowed to drive along it.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on Triq ir-Repubblika, about 30 m south-west of the subject, and face north-east. Keep to the side of the street so you're not in the way of people walking or a passing karozzin.

card.hook: Picture three bronze Tritons holding up a fountain, with a huge modern gate sitting behind them like a picture frame. That's your shot, and it's right at the front door of Valletta.
card.stand_here: Walk to the Triton Fountain, just outside the gate, and stand directly in front of it. Face the City Gate, so the Tritons and their basin fill the bottom of your picture.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the fountain, the gate and some of the old walls in one go. Then switch to 1x for a tighter, tidier picture.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the fountain in the lower part of the frame with the gate opening in the middle, and keep your phone level so the walls stay straight.
card.best_time: Go early, before about 8:30, when the light is good and the square is almost empty. The fountain is lit after dark too, and plenty of visitors love it then (use night mode and rest your elbows on something solid).
card.selfie_here: Stay at the Triton Fountain and stand in the open area in front of it, with your back to the City Gate. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold the phone a bit higher so the gate's entrance shows over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the bridge that leads up to the gate and shoot back toward it, while you stand at the gate's entrance so the whole structure fits in.
card.rules_and_safety: The fountain is in an open pedestrian square and the gate is the public entrance to the city, but check the official site before you go in case of works or closures.
card.challenge: Can you get all three Tritons, the gate opening and your own grin into one straight, level shot? Take three tries and pick the winner.
card.good_to_know: The Maltese name is Bieb il-Belt, 'Door of the City'. The first gate here dates from 1569 and was called Porta San Giorgio. The one you see today is the fifth on this spot, designed by Renzo Piano and finished in 2014.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk to the Triton Fountain, just outside the gate, and stand directly in front of it. Face the City Gate, so the Tritons and their basin fill the bottom of your picture. Don't shoot from the phone icon itself.

card.hook: Picture slim iron columns marching down a bright hall, a timber-decked iron roof overhead, and someone choosing lunch right underneath it. That's Is-Suq tal-Belt, and it's a lot more photogenic than your average food court.
card.stand_here: Stand right inside Is-Suq tal-Belt in Valletta. The phone icon on the map marks the spot, which puts you in the middle of the building. Turn around slowly and pick the direction that shows the most roof and the longest line of columns.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the full length of the hall and its iron roof in one shot. Switch to 1x for stalls and people, then try 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) for column tops, signs and food.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the rows of iron columns with the vertical lines so the whole hall stands up straight.
card.best_time: Go outside the busiest meal times and you'll get clear views without crowds in your shot. Daylight coming through the building makes the iron structure look its best.
card.selfie_here: Head up to the open upper-floor seating area inside the market hall, not street level, for a Victorian-style selfie. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x and tilt it so the iron roof and columns sit over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Be polite when photographing stallholders and other visitors, and ask first if you want a close portrait. Opening times can change, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find the most colourful food display in the hall and get one photo of it with a column lined up perfectly straight behind it.
card.good_to_know: The hall was built between 1859 and 1861 and was the first building in Malta made mostly of prefabricated iron. Its design took ideas from Covent Garden in London and the Halles Centrales in Paris. It was badly bombed in 1942 and lost about a third of its structure, then was renovated in 2016-17 and reopened in January 2018.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right inside Is-Suq tal-Belt in Valletta. The phone icon on the map marks the spot, which puts you in the middle of the building. Turn around slowly and pick the direction that shows the most roof and the longest line of columns.

card.hook: This building has two old cannons guarding the front door and a bronze bust perched above it, so it's basically begging for a photo. It also sits at the highest point of Valletta, so it knows it's the star.
card.stand_here: Walk to the phone icon on the map, near Misraħ Kastilja, about 50 m south-west of the Auberge de Castille. Face north-east and the whole front is ahead of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the whole façade in one frame. If you end up standing close, switch to 0.5x. Then zoom to 2x for the doorway, the bronze bust and the coats of arms.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the building, then drag the slider to darker if the pale stone looks washed out against the sky.
card.best_time: Go in the morning or late afternoon, when the softer, lower light brings out the carving in the stone. Take a few shots, because passers-by love to wander through the frame.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the front step beside the cannons with the doorway behind you, if the cannons are still there. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold it a little low so the façade fits over your shoulder. The open square in front also works, with the building behind you and the busy street scene in front.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to back away a few steps into the open part of the square so the whole front fits in the frame, while you stand on the front step by the doorway.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a working government building, so stick to photos from outside. Avoid photographing sensitive areas or personnel, and be respectful if a ceremonial guard is posted outside.
card.challenge: Count the bays across the façade in your photo. If you get eleven, give yourself a gold star.
card.good_to_know: The Auberge de Castille was built in the Spanish Baroque style between 1741 and 1744 under Grand Master Manuel Pinto da Fonseca. It replaced a 1570s auberge by Girolamo Cassar and was originally a base for knights from Castile, León and Portugal. Today it houses the Office of the Prime Minister, and locals often just say "Castille" to mean that office.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk to the phone icon on the map, near Misraħ Kastilja, about 50 m south-west of the Auberge de Castille. Face north-east and the whole front is ahead of you.

card.hook: Nobody tells you that one of Valletta's prettiest church fronts is hiding in a street so narrow you'll feel like you're photographing it from inside a cupboard. Don't worry, it's worth the shuffle.
card.stand_here: Stand on Triq San Pawl, directly opposite the church facade across the narrow street, and face north-west. From there you can see the tall, slim Baroque front and its twin belfries framed by old stone buildings.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x if the street feels too tight to fit the whole front, then try 1x from the far side of the street. Switch to zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the belfries and the carved detail.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the facade up with the vertical lines so the walls don't lean.
card.best_time: Daylight is easiest, because the front is evenly lit. The light in a narrow street changes quickly, so check your screen and retake if one side is in deep shade. In the evening, try night mode and rest your phone against a wall or railing to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera and step back as far as the street comfortably allows, then tuck the church over your shoulder. Try zoom 0.5x if your phone has it on the front camera, but keep your face away from the edges so it doesn't stretch.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working parish church, so check the official site for visiting times and photo rules. Photography inside may be allowed for personal use, but not during services, so check on the day.
card.challenge: Get the whole front in with both walls standing perfectly straight and not a single passer-by in the doorway. Patience is the real skill here.
card.good_to_know: The church goes back to the 1570s, was designed by Girolamo Cassar and was finished in December 1582. The facade you see today is later: it was rebuilt in 1885 to a design by Nicholas Zammit. Inside is a wooden statue of St Paul carved in 1659 by Melchiorre Cafà, which is carried through Valletta's streets on the feast day, 10 February.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Triq San Pawl, directly opposite the church facade across the narrow street, and face north-west. From there you can see the tall, slim Baroque front and its twin belfries framed by old stone buildings.

rules.rule: Tripods are not allowed during church services; personal photography inside is otherwise allowed.

card.hook: Picture a grand theatre with no roof, where the only ceiling is the Maltese sky. That's the Royal Opera House ruins, just inside Valletta's entrance, and the old stone tells its story without any help from you.
card.stand_here: Stand in Pjazza Teatru Rjal and face across the restored ruins toward the stage. You want the surviving columns lined up against the modern stage and seating, with the city beyond.
card.zoom: The site is about 95 m across, so start at zoom 0.5x to fit as much as you can in one go. Then try 1x for a calmer, more natural view. If your phone has 2x or 5x, use it to pick out the texture of the stone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up any upright stonework with the vertical lines so nothing leans.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and gentler shadows on the stone. Midday sun can make the pale stone look flat and harsh.
card.selfie_here: Head for the paved terrace in Pjazza Teatru Rjal and stand with the surviving columns directly behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if you want more of the ruins in, and hold the phone a little higher. The staircase leading up to the ruins is a second option, and it gives you a different angle from above ground level.
card.ask_someone: Stand on Republic Street near the city gate end with the ruins behind you, and ask a passer-by to shoot back toward you from the street so the columns fill the frame (it's a suggestion, so check it on the ground).
card.rules_and_safety: It's a public city-centre site that's also used as a performance venue, so check the official site before you go in case an event limits access.
card.challenge: Wait for a gap in the crowd, then get one person standing small against the columns so the size of the place really shows.
card.good_to_know: The theatre was designed by the English architect Edward Middleton Barry and opened in 1866 with seats for 1,095 people. It was devastated by wartime bombing in April 1942. Today Renzo Piano's open-air design, opened in 2013, fills the site as Pjazza Teatru Rjal.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Pjazza Teatru Rjal and face across the restored ruins toward the stage. You want the surviving columns lined up against the modern stage and seating, with the city beyond.

card.hook: Republic Street is Valletta's busiest street, so someone will walk through your photo. Good news: the library's calm, symmetrical front, with Queen Victoria standing guard, can handle a crowd.
card.stand_here: Stand in Republic Square (Misrah ir-Repubblika), across the square from the main facade, with the Queen Victoria statue in front of you. From the Grandmaster's Palace area, the library is to the south-east of it, about 1 minute on foot. Face the library's front.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole facade with the statue in front. If you have to stand close, switch to 0.5x to keep the whole front in the frame. Then try zoom 2x or more (depending on your phone) for the arches and the doorway.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the columns up with the vertical lines so the building doesn't lean, with the statue slightly off-centre in the lower part of the frame.
card.best_time: Go early in the day or later in the afternoon, when there are fewer people on Republic Street and in the square. Take two or three frames anyway, because people keep walking through.
card.selfie_here: Walk to the main entrance and stand under the arched gallery, which an audio tour calls a perfect photo spot. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and let the library's facade sit behind your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand out on the open square facing the library (Café Cordina is directly opposite), while you pose in front of the building so the whole facade fits behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is not allowed inside the library, so keep your pictures to the outside. The exterior and the statue are fine to photograph. Check the official site for opening arrangements before you go.
card.challenge: Find a gap between passers-by and shoot through it for a wide shot, then step closer and frame the doorway through the arches.
card.good_to_know: The Bibliotheca was founded in 1776 by Grand Master Emmanuel de Rohan-Polduc. Stefano Ittar designed it, and his son Sebastiano carried on after Stefano died. It was finished in 1796 but not opened until 1812, and it's an early example of neoclassical architecture in Malta and a Grade 1 national monument.

card.hook: Two shapes poke up above Valletta's rooftops: a big oval dome and a slim spire, and the dome is reportedly built to win the height contest by a hair.
card.stand_here: Stand at Tigné Point on the Sliema side and face south across Marsamxett Harbour. Look for the dome with the spire right beside it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to catch the whole skyline, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to bring the dome closer. Use 0.5x only if you want lots of water and sky.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the dome, then slide it a little darker so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Go about an hour before sunset, when the low light warms the sandstone buildings. Stay on into blue hour, when the sky behind the dome looks its best.
card.selfie_here: Try the Tigné seafront promenade in Sliema, with your back to the harbour so Valletta and the dome sit behind you. Use the front camera (0.5x if your phone has it) and tilt it up so the dome peeks over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back from the water's edge while you stand between them and the skyline, so the dome sits right behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Getting to Tigné Point involves steep stairs, so take your time. The church itself is a place of worship, so check the official site before you visit.
card.challenge: Line up the dome and spire on one gridline, keep the horizon dead level, and save a strip of water at the bottom. Bonus points if nobody's thumb is in it.
card.good_to_know: The church is young: it was built between 1958 and 1981, on the site of a late 16th-century church badly damaged by bombing in March 1942. The dome is about 42 m high and faces Marsamxett Harbour. It was reportedly designed to sit slightly higher than the bell tower of nearby St Paul's Pro-Cathedral.

card.hook: Locals have called this building a cheese grater, a dovecote and a honeycomb, and it caused plenty of argument when it went up. Your phone will love it anyway: strong shapes, repeating patterns and lots of texture.
card.stand_here: The building lies to the north-west, about 30 minutes on foot. Stand in the open area near City Gate on Republic Street and face it from the side or at an angle, not straight on.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the whole building and its surroundings. If you're close to the staircase and can't fit the front in, try 0.5x. For the carved limestone details, go to 2x or more, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the stonework, then slide the picture a touch darker so the pale limestone keeps its texture.
card.best_time: Go mid-morning, when the sun shades half of the steps. The staircase and entrance are usually busy, so be patient and shoot between groups of people.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie on the Parliament House staircase, where travel blogs say the sun shades half of the steps mid-morning. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the building behind your shoulder. Crowds on the steps can make a solo shot harder, so wait for a gap.
card.rules_and_safety: Most of the building is closed to visitors, though a ground-floor exhibition is open to the public. Photography inside may be restricted, so keep your main pictures for outside.
card.challenge: Take two pictures: one wide shot of the whole building in its setting, and one close-up of the stonework. Then decide for yourself if it looks more like a honeycomb or a cheese grater.
card.good_to_know: Parliament House was built between 2011 and 2015 and designed by the architect Renzo Piano. The limestone came from Gozo, and the carved slabs are meant to look eroded by nature. The two blocks are kept apart so that views of Saint James Cavalier from Republic Street stay open.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: The building lies to the north-west, about 30 minutes on foot. Stand in the open area near City Gate on Republic Street and face it from the side or at an angle, not straight on.

card.hook: Find the slimmest spike on Valletta's skyline and you've found St Paul's spire, the one that looks like it's trying to out-tall the domes. It's over 60 metres of Maltese limestone, and it's surprisingly easy to spot from across the water.
card.stand_here: Head for the Tigné Point terrace, at the last tip of Sliema on the far side of the harbour from Valletta. Face south across the water and look for the spire beside the Carmelite dome. The church itself is in Independence Square, so check the map to see which side of the harbour you're on.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole skyline in. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to squeeze the spire and the dome closer together. Use 0.5x only if you want loads of sky and harbour, because the church will look tiny.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the sunlit stonework, then slide it a touch darker so the sky keeps its colour and the walls don't wash out.
card.best_time: Go about an hour before sunset, when the stone turns warm and golden. Stay on into blue hour, switch on night mode and rest your elbows on the railing or a wall to keep things sharp.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold it a little higher than usual. Turn so the skyline sits over your shoulder and the spire pokes up beside your head.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Old Theatre Street and frame the whole church, with you in front of it.
card.rules_and_safety: If you go inside, personal photography is allowed but flash is discouraged. Check the official site first, as indoor photos may need a donation.
card.challenge: Get the spire and the Carmelite dome side by side, with the skyline sitting on the lower third of your screen. Bonus points if the water is calm enough to give you a little reflection.
card.good_to_know: Dowager Queen Adelaide commissioned the church because Anglicans on the island had nowhere of their own to worship. William Scamp designed it, and it was built between 1839 and 1844 on the site of the old Auberge d'Allemagne. A restoration of the building and steeple was completed in 2024.

card.hook: Most grand buildings shout. The Auberge d'Aragon just stands there, one storey of plain limestone, and somehow that's what makes it great for a photo.
card.stand_here: Stand in Misraħ Indipendenza, the open square in front of the main façade. The auberge lies to the north-east of the square, about 1 minute on foot, so face north-east and you'll see the whole front.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the full low front in one shot. Try zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the portico, the cornice or the rough-cut corners. If you're tight against the building, as on Archbishop Street, switch to zoom 0.5x.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the cornice up with a horizontal line so the building doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually suits pale limestone better than harsh midday sun. Early in the day the square is likely to be quieter too.
card.selfie_here: Use the open square in front of the building, on the piazza in front of the Doric portico, with the façade behind you. Use the front camera, switch to zoom 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the portico over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back across the square from the portico, far enough that the whole front fits, while you stand in front of the portico facing them.
card.rules_and_safety: You can photograph the outside from the square and street, but it's a working government office and not generally open to the public. Inside photos are only allowed during select events. If you fly a drone, check the local restrictions first.
card.challenge: Get the cornice dead straight on a gridline, then count the three windows on each side of the door. Do they look perfectly matched to you?
card.good_to_know: The auberge was built from 1571 for knights of the Order of Saint John from Aragon, Navarre and Catalonia, and the architect was Girolamo Cassar. It's the only auberge in Valletta that still has its original Mannerist design. The Doric portico was added around 1842, when it was known as Gibraltar House, and since 2020 the building has housed the Ministry for Justice.
